info.title: NexQ
info.description: The native REST API for NexQ, a multi-protocol queue server. It covers every operation NexQ supports — including the features that go beyond what the SQS-compatible endpoint can express — and is the API to reach for when you are writing against NexQ directly rather than through an AWS SDK.

get.description:
In name order, one page at a time, optionally filtered by `prefix`. Add `?counts=true` for each queue's message counts — off by default because it costs one aggregate *per queue on the page*, so a page of a thousand asks for a thousand of them.

When `nextCursor` is not null there are more: pass it back as `cursor` to continue. It is a **cursor, not an offset** — it names where to resume, so a queue created or deleted between two requests cannot make you skip one or see it twice. That is the storage layer's keyset guarantee carried onto the wire rather than re-derived from it, and it is why there is no "page number".

A cursor is this server's to issue. Constructing one yourself is not supported and is refused rather than interpreted. An empty result is a normal answer, not an error.

get.description:
Returns the queue's name, when it was created, when its attributes were last changed, and those attributes.

Add `?counts=true` for how many messages it holds, in three disjoint groups that together cover all of them: claimable now, in flight with a live claim, and waiting out a delay. Off by default because it costs an aggregate over the queue's messages, which is nearly free against the in-memory backend and not necessarily against a durable one.

put.summary: Create a queue, or confirm one exists
put.description:
Creates the queue named in the path. `PUT` rather than a `POST` to the collection because the operation is idempotent and the client chooses the name: sending the same request twice leaves one queue, not two.

Sending it again with the *same* attributes returns the existing queue, because the intent — "there should be a queue called this, configured like this" — is already satisfied. Sending it with *different* attributes is a conflict rather than a reconfiguration, since silently retiming a queue consumers are working would be worse than refusing.

Every attribute is optional and falls back to the server's default. An attribute outside its range is refused rather than clamped, and one this server does not implement is refused rather than ignored, so a setting never looks applied when it was dropped.

requestBody.description:
Settings to create a queue with. Every field is optional and falls back to the
 server's default. An unrecognised field is refused rather than ignored, so a setting
 never looks applied when it was dropped.

default.description:
The body of every failed request.

 Nested under `error` rather than flattened so that a successful response and a failed
 one can never be told apart only by which fields happen to be present.

200.description: The queue, whether it was just created or already existed.

400.description: The name is not a legal queue name, or an attribute is outside its range or not one this server implements.

409.description: A queue of that name exists with different attributes.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

415.description: A body was sent as something other than `application/json`. Send no body at all to accept the defaults.

delete.description:
Deletes the queue and everything in it, **including messages a consumer is currently holding** — a receipt handle taken across this stops working, because the message it referred to is gone. Consumers long-polling on the queue are released rather than left waiting on something that no longer exists.

Not idempotent in the way `PUT` is: deleting a queue that was never there is a `404`, because a caller in that position has a different problem from one whose delete worked.

default.description:
The body of every failed request.

 Nested under `error` rather than flattened so that a successful response and a failed
 one can never be told apart only by which fields happen to be present.

204.description: The queue is gone. No body.

400.description: The name is not a legal queue name.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

patch.description:
A **partial** update: an attribute this body does not name keeps its current value rather than reverting to a default. That is the whole difference from `PUT`, which says what a queue should *be* — so `PUT` with one attribute resets the others and `PATCH` with one attribute leaves them alone.

All-or-nothing: a request mixing a valid attribute with an invalid one changes neither, so you are never left with half a change applied. A request naming no attributes at all is refused rather than treated as a no-op that still moves `lastModifiedAt`.

Only the three attributes this server has behaviour behind can be set. One it does not implement is refused rather than accepted and ignored.

post.description:
Takes a **list**, always. Sending one message is a list of one — there is no separate batch operation to choose between, which is one fewer thing to get wrong than the SQS pair it replaces.

Not a transaction. Each message is accepted or refused on its own and the response reports both, so nine good messages are not lost to one bad one. The request itself is a `200` in that case, so **read the results** rather than relying on an error being raised. Entries are identified by their position in the request, so unlike SQS there are no ids to supply and no duplicate-id failure.

`priority` is NexQ's own and one of the reasons this API exists: the SQS-compatible facade cannot express it, so messages sent through that one all arrive at the default. Higher is served first.

A queue that does not exist is one raised `404` rather than the same failure repeated in every entry, because the queue belongs to the request and not to any message in it.

200.description: One result per message, in request order. Some may be refused — check `status` on each.

400.description: The list is empty or too long, the queue name is not legal, or the body does not fit the schema. Nothing was sent.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

415.description: A body was sent as something other than `application/json`. Send no body at all to accept the defaults.

delete.summary: Throw away every message in a queue
delete.description:
Empties the queue and keeps the queue — `DELETE` on the *message collection*, where deleting the queue itself is `DELETE` one level up.

**Irreversible, and it takes in-flight messages with it**: a consumer working on a message right now will find its receipt handle refused, because the message is gone. A purge that spared claimed messages would be one that quietly did not purge, since those messages would reappear when their claims lapsed.

Unlike SQS there is no sixty-second cooldown. SQS needs one because its purge runs asynchronously and it refuses a second while the first is still going; this one has finished by the time it answers, so refusing would be a limitation invented for its own sake. The count of what went is returned, and logged.

default.description:
The body of every failed request.

 Nested under `error` rather than flattened so that a successful response and a failed
 one can never be told apart only by which fields happen to be present.

400.description: The queue name is not legal.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

post.description:
Claims up to `maxMessages` messages, making them invisible to other consumers until the claim lapses or they are deleted. A `POST` because it changes something: two identical calls return different messages.

With `waitTimeSeconds` the request is held open until a message arrives or the wait runs out — long polling — and returns the moment one is sent, including one sent through the SQS-compatible facade, since both run over one queue. Omitting it uses the queue's own configured wait, which is a different thing from sending `0`: zero asks for a plain poll. The wait applies to the *first* message only, so asking for ten when three exist returns three rather than holding on for seven more.

An empty list is a normal answer, not an error — including when a long poll runs out, and when the server is shutting down and releases waiting consumers.

Every message comes with a receipt handle identifying **that claim**, not the message: a redelivery arrives with a new one. There is no way to delete a message through this facade yet, so a claim taken here lapses and the message returns; use the SQS facade to delete it.

post.description:
The same as deleting one message, several at a time. A `POST` rather than a `DELETE` carrying a body, since a body on `DELETE` is legal but widely mishandled by proxies and clients.

Not a transaction: each handle succeeds or fails on its own and the response reports both, identified by position. A handle whose claim already ended is refused as itself rather than sinking the rest.

400.description: The list is empty or too long, or the queue name is not legal.

post.description:
The same as re-timing one claim, several at a time, each with its own timeout. Not a transaction: outcomes are per entry and identified by position.

Unlike the SQS operation this replaces, a timeout is required on every entry rather than optional — there is no queue default to fall back to that would not be a guess about what the caller meant.

The body of every failed request.

200.description: One result per change, in request order.

400.description: The list is empty or too long, or the queue name is not legal.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

415.description: A body was sent as something other than `application/json`. Send no body at all to accept the defaults.

delete.description:
Deletes the message a receipt handle refers to, which is how a consumer says it is done. Until this happens the message comes back when its claim lapses — that is what makes delivery at-least-once.

The handle identifies **one claim**, not the message. A handle whose claim has already ended — deleted, or lapsed so the message went to another consumer — is refused rather than silently doing nothing, since a consumer that has lost its claim needs to know it may have duplicated work.

parameters.name: receiptHandle
parameters.description:
The receipt handle a receive handed out. It identifies one claim, not the message,
 so it stops working when that claim ends.

schema.description:
The receipt handle a receive handed out. It identifies one claim, not the message,
 so it stops working when that claim ends.

default.description:
The body of every failed request.

 Nested under `error` rather than flattened so that a successful response and a failed
 one can never be told apart only by which fields happen to be present.

204.description: The message is gone. No body.

400.description: The queue name is not legal, or the receipt handle does not identify a current claim.

401.description: The bearer token is missing or does not check out.

patch.description:
Sets how much longer a claim lasts, **counted from now** rather than from when the message was received. One operation for two jobs, which is what makes that choice the useful one: a consumer that needs longer extends its claim instead of having the message handed to someone else mid-work, and a consumer that cannot do the work at all sets `0`.

`0` hands the message straight back, and because that is a client action making a message claimable it **wakes a consumer that is long-polling** for one — work returned by one consumer reaches the next without waiting out a timeout.

The receipt handle stays valid on a non-zero change: this alters when a claim ends, not whose it is.

bearerAuth.description: The token is `<key_id>.<secret>` for a credential in the server's registry. Presented in full on every request, so it should travel over TLS.

AttributeType.description:
What kind of value an attribute carries.

 Three kinds, matching what the SQS facade accepts, so an attribute set here survives a
 round trip through that facade unchanged.

oneOf.description: A number, still written as text so no precision is lost on the way through JSON.

ClaimPath.description: Which claim a request is about.

receiptHandle.description:
The receipt handle a receive handed out. It identifies one claim, not the message,
 so it stops working when that claim ends.

receiptHandles.description: The claims to finish, by receipt handle.

EntryResult.description:
What happened to one entry.

 **A request carrying several entries is not a transaction**: each succeeds or fails on
 its own and the response reports both, so nine good messages are not lost to one bad
 one. The request itself is still a `200` — a client has to read the results rather than
 rely on an error being raised.

index.description:
Which entry this is, by position in the request's list. Positions rather than
 client-supplied ids: an array already has them, and SQS's duplicate-id failure
 cannot happen.

messageId.description: The id of the accepted message, for a send.

status.description: Whether it was accepted. Exactly one of `messageId` and `error` accompanies it.

EntryResults.description: What happened to each entry of a multi-entry request.

results.description: One per entry, in request order.

EntryStatus.description: Whether one entry of a multi-entry request was accepted.

The body of every failed request.

 Nested under `error` rather than flattened so that a successful response and a failed
 one can never be told apart only by which fields happen to be present.

code.description: A stable, machine-readable identifier for this kind of failure. Safe to branch on.

message.description: A human-readable explanation. May change between releases; do not parse it.

ListQueuesQuery.description: Which queues to list, and where to resume.

counts.description:
Include message counts for every queue on the page.

 Off by default: it costs one aggregate per queue, so a page of a thousand asks for
 a thousand of them. Ask for it when you are showing depths, not by habit.

cursor.description: Resume after this queue — the `nextCursor` from the previous page.

limit.description: How many to return at most.

prefix.description: Only queues whose name starts with this.

nextCursor.description:
Pass as `cursor` to fetch the next page, or `null` when this is the last one.

 A **cursor**, not an offset: it names where to resume, so a queue created or
 deleted between pages cannot make a caller skip one or see it twice. Present
 whenever more remain, including when `limit` was not given.

queues.description: This page, in name order. Empty rather than absent when there are none.

MessageAttributeBody.description:
One piece of metadata the producer attached to a message.

 The value is always a JSON string. For `binary` it is base64 of the bytes, which is
 what keeps the wire format one shape instead of two — and the bytes are what is stored,
 so text that happens to look like base64 and the bytes it decodes to stay different
 things.

label.description:
An optional label of the producer's own, describing the value more precisely — a
 `string` labelled `uuid`, say. Carried through untouched and given back on receive.

value.description: The value: text for `string` and `number`, base64 for `binary`.

MessageCountsResponse.description:
How many messages a queue holds, in three disjoint groups that together cover all of
 them.

delayed.description: Waiting out a delay, and never yet delivered.

notVisible.description: In flight: handed to a consumer whose claim has not lapsed, and not yet deleted.

total.description: The three above added up — every message the queue holds.

PurgeResponse.description: How much a purge threw away.

purged.description: Messages removed, counting ones a consumer was holding.

QueueAttributesBody.description:
Settings to create a queue with. Every field is optional and falls back to the
 server's default. An unrecognised field is refused rather than ignored, so a setting
 never looks applied when it was dropped.

receiveWaitTimeSeconds.description: Defaults to none, which makes a receive a plain poll unless it asks to wait.

delaySeconds.description: How long a newly sent message waits before it can be received.

receiveWaitTimeSeconds.description:
How long a receive that finds nothing waits by default — the long poll a consumer
 gets without asking for one.

visibilityTimeoutSeconds.description:
How long a claimed message stays invisible to other consumers before being
 redelivered.

QueuePath.description:
The queue a request is about.

 A struct rather than `Path<String>` because that is what lets the parameter be
 *documented*: from a bare `String` aide learns a path parameter exists but not what it
 is called, and generates an operation with no parameters at all. The field name is the
 parameter name.

QueueResponse.description: A queue, as this API represents it.

counts.description:
How many messages the queue holds, present only when `counts=true` was asked for.

 Off by default because it costs an aggregate over the queue's messages — once per
 queue, so asking for it while listing a thousand queues asks for a thousand of them.
 Cheap against the in-memory backend and not necessarily against a durable one.

lastModifiedAt.description:
When its attributes were last changed, or when it was created if they never have
 been. Reported separately because answering with the creation time for both would
 be a plausible-looking lie.

name.description: The queue's name, which is also its address: `/api/v1/queues/{name}`.

QueueViewQuery.description: How much of a queue to report.

ReceiveBody.description:
What a consumer may ask for. Every field is optional; an empty body is a plain poll of
 one message under the queue's own defaults.

maxMessages.description:
How many messages to return at most. Fewer may come back, including none.

 Defaults to one when omitted. A value outside the range is refused rather than
 clamped, so asking for more than the maximum is an error and not a short answer.

visibilityTimeoutSeconds.description:
How long the returned messages stay invisible to other consumers.

 Omitted means the queue's own configured timeout.

waitTimeSeconds.description:
How long to wait for a message when the queue has none — long polling.

 Omitted means the queue's own configured wait, which is a different thing from
 `0`: zero asks for a plain poll that returns immediately.

messages.description:
Claimed messages, **empty rather than absent** when there are none.

 SQS omits the field entirely in that case, which is a quirk clients have to be
 written around; a native API has no reason to repeat it. An empty list is a normal
 answer, not an error, including when a long poll times out.

ReceivedMessage.description: One message, and the claim it came with.

attributes.description:
Whatever metadata the producer attached, keyed by name.

 Always present, and empty for a message carrying none — always returned in full
 rather than only when asked for, since a consumer that did not want them can ignore
 a map it already has, while one that did would otherwise need a second request.

body.description: The message body, exactly as it was sent.

claimExpiresInSeconds.description:
How long this claim has left.

 A duration rather than an absolute expiry time on purpose: a consumer needs to
 know how long it has, and answering that with a timestamp makes the answer depend
 on the client's clock agreeing with the server's. Saturates at zero rather than
 going negative if the claim lapsed while the response was being written.

id.description:
The message's identifier, stable across redeliveries. The same value the
 SQS-compatible facade reports as `MessageId`.

priority.description:
Higher is served first. Messages sent through the SQS facade all carry the
 default, since that protocol cannot express a priority.

receiptHandle.description:
The token to present to delete this message or change its visibility. Refers to
 *this claim*, not to the message: a redelivery comes with a new one.

receiveCount.description: How many times this message has been delivered, counting this delivery.

messages.description:
One or more messages. Sending a single message is a list of one — there is no
 separate batch operation to choose between.

attributes.description: Metadata to carry alongside the body, keyed by name.

delaySeconds.description:
Hold this message back for this long before any consumer can receive it.

 Overrides the queue's own delay for this message alone.

priority.description:
Higher is served first; defaults to the middle of the road.

 NexQ's own concept, and one of the reasons this API exists: the SQS-compatible
 facade cannot express it, so messages sent through that one all arrive at the
 default.

VisibilityBody.description: A new visibility timeout for one claim.

visibilityTimeoutSeconds.description:
How much longer the claim should last, counted from now.

 `0` hands the message straight back, which wakes a consumer waiting for one.
How much longer it should last, counted from now.
